name: Classical Sicilian
summary: The Classical Sicilian develops both knights to c6 and f6, a flexible system that can steer into the Richter-Rauzer, Dragon, or Boleslavsky lines.
intro: The Classical Sicilian is reached after 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 Nc6, when both of Black's knights come out to their most natural squares, f6 and c6, before Black commits to a precise plan. It is one of the oldest and most principled ways to handle the Open Sicilian, aiming for harmonious development and pressure on White's e4-pawn and the d4-knight. The move order is highly flexible: depending on White's sixth move the game can turn into the Richter-Rauzer after 6.Bg5, the sharp Sozin with 6.Bc4, or a Boleslavsky-style structure if Black is allowed to play ...e5. Rich in transpositional possibilities, the Classical is a mainstay of tournament practice at every level.
line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 Nc6

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: Black adopts the small-centre Sicilian structure with pawns on d6 and, soon, e6 or e5, trusting piece activity and the half-open c-file to generate counterplay. The knight on c6 pressures d4 and can be exchanged or driven back, while the f6-knight bears down on e4 and eyes the key d5- and e4-squares. Development is quick and solid, and the choice between a small centre with ...e6 and a big-centre grab with ...e5 defines much of the coming middlegame. On the c-file the rook and the queen, often via ...Qc7 or ...Qa5, look for counterplay against c3 and c2.

A defining decision is whether Black plays ...e5 to seize central space, as in the Boleslavsky system. This gains room and activates the pieces but concedes the d5-square as a permanent outpost, and the resulting battle turns on whether White can exploit the d5-hole with a knight or whether Black's active pieces and pressure down the half-open files compensate. If instead Black keeps a small centre with ...e6, the play resembles the Scheveningen and Rauzer structures, with slow manoeuvring and opposite-wing plans. White enjoys a lead in space and must choose between quiet development and a direct attacking scheme.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: White's most testing try is 6.Bg5, the Richter-Rauzer Attack, pinning the f6-knight and preparing Qd2 and long castling with attacking chances against Black's king. The alternative 6.Bc4 is the Sozin, and with a later ...e6 the Fischer-Sozin, aiming the bishop at f7 and the a2-g8 diagonal for a sharp assault. Both lines have generated enormous theory and remain fully topical.

The quieter 6.Be2 invites 6...e5, the Boleslavsky Variation, where Black stakes a claim in the centre and accepts the d5-hole in exchange for free-flowing piece play. White may also try 6.Be3 with f3 and a slow build-up, or 6.g3 to fianchetto and fight for d5 positionally. Because so many of these systems can arise from other Sicilian move orders, the Classical is prized as much for its flexibility as for any single main line.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Classical Sicilian is among the oldest branches of the Open Sicilian, its natural developing scheme dating back to the nineteenth century and refined steadily through the twentieth. The Soviet grandmaster Isaac Boleslavsky did more than anyone to shape modern understanding of the ...e5 structures in the late 1940s and 1950s, and the central pawn formation he championed still bears his name.

Over the decades the variation has been employed by a long line of leading players, and its Richter-Rauzer and Sozin branches in particular became battlegrounds of top-level theory. Its enduring appeal lies in the naturalness of the setup and the wealth of pawn structures it can reach, making it both a practical fighting choice and a rich field for opening study.
